Title: Empowering Generative AI in Enterprises: Sustainable, High-Performance Storage Solutions with Global Data Fabric and Data Lakehouse

Abstract
Rapid growth in unstructured data has triggered enterprises to shift
from traditional file storage to scalable object storage solutions
in their infrastructure. There has been a growing need to inte-
grate both file and object storage into a unified platform capable of
managing the complexities of traditional and modern data work-
loads. Gartner predicts that by 2029, over 80% of unstructured data
will reside on consolidated storage systems—up from 40% in early
2024—highlighting the urgency of this transition. As sustainability
takes center stage, businesses must adopt storage solutions that
deliver both high performance and minimal environmental impact.
This paper presents a storage solution designed for Generative AI
and High-Performance Computing (HPC), addressing two critical
requirements:
1. A unified high-performance storage solution that seamlessly
integrates both file and object storage access.
2. A sustainable approach to building infrastructure that re-
duces energy usage and carbon emissions.
We will explore how sustainable, high-performance storage solu-
tions such as global data fabrics and data lakehouse technologies
enable this vision. Key topics include:
1. The critical role of efficient storage in accelerating AI work-
loads.
2. The advantages of distributed file and object storage for
enterprise-scale workloads.
3. Essential sustainability practices that align with environ-
mental goals.
4. A global data fabric use case, leveraging features from refer-
ence architectures for research data, that incorporates these
innovations as well as embedded sustainability practices.
This paper demonstrates how researchers, architects, CIOs, and
administrators can leverage next-generation storage solutions to
improve operational efficiency and support sustainability in gener-
ative AI use cases.

1
Introduction
The rapid expansion of unstructured data has driven organizations
to move beyond traditional file-based systems toward more scalable
and versatile solutions. Object storage has become standard for
handling these vast amounts of data, resulting in data silos and
duplication. Integration of both file and object storage into a single,
unified platform addresses the challenges posed by diverse and
complex workloads, enabling organizations to access data in both
formats without duplication and inefficiencies.
As data grows rapidly [1], Gartner forecasts [2] that by 2029, over
80% of unstructured data will be stored on consolidated systems—
up from just 40% in early 2024. Enterprises must urgently adopt
storage solutions for unified data access that combine performance,
scalability, and cost-efficiency. As sustainability considerations
have become important in infrastructure building, organizations
must also prioritize eco-friendly solutions that reduce energy con-
sumption and carbon emissions. In this paper, we provide informa-
tion about designing storage architectures for Generative AI and
High-Performance Computing (HPC) workloads. This addresses
two critical, interrelated needs:

that seamlessly integrates both file and object storage.
2. A sustainable storage solution that minimizes energy usage
while delivering appropriate performance for the use cases
intended.
This paper presents a next-generation storage solution utiliz-
ing global data fabric [3] and data lakehouse [4] technologies that
can enable AI workloads, accelerate enterprise workflows, and
contribute to environmental goals. We also draw insights from
a Reference Architecture for Research Data [5], which highlights
contemporary storage demands, further validating the importance
of this integrated, sustainable approach in tackling real-world chal-
lenges.
2
Problem statement
An urgent need for unified storage solutions that support both
file and object data access has become apparent, driven by the
increasing adoption of Generative AI and the associated High-
Performance Computing requirements. Traditional storage systems
remain siloed, operating separately for file and object data.
Organizations face two primary challenges:
1. Lack of Unified Storage for File and Object Access: The
inability to access the same dataset seamlessly through both
file and object protocols results in operational silos and sig-
nificant resource duplication. This fragmentation introduces
inefficiencies, delays, unnecessary staff and infrastructure
costs, and opportunities for errors due to both machine-and
user-related failures in data movement, and thus limits the
agility required for high-performance workloads. A unified,
high-performance storage solution avoids the complexity
of managing separate storage platforms, allowing organiza-
tions to better handle the increasing demands of AI and HPC
workflows.
2. Environmental Sustainability and Energy Consump-
tion: As data storage deployments expand in scale, so too
does the associated energy consumption. The associated
cost and environmental impacts create a pressing need to
combine sustainability with performance. Without a focus
on minimizing energy usage and carbon emissions, busi-
nesses may fail to meet environmental goals, thus risking
both financial and reputational harm.
This paper demonstrates how organizations can bridge the gap
between performance and sustainability. The Reference Architec-
ture for Research Data [5] also emphasizes the importance of a
storage system that has features that provide high-performance,
appropriate flexibility, scalability and resiliency to meet the grow-
ing demands of AI and HPC research environments, while also
reducing environmental impact.
3
METHOD
The aim is to achieve a sustainable, high-performance consolidated
storage system by integrating sustainability principles with a stor-
age platform capable of delivering high-performance access to data
in both file and object formats. This goal is realized through the
implementation the various approaches for a data lakehouse archi-
tecture, which offers a flexible and efficient approach to managing
storage infrastructure while promoting sustainability.
An example of this might be a large media enterprise operating
a workflow where users write data via NFS (Network File System
protocol) to a file storage system. That data is subsequently copied
to object storage, against which a high-performance computer
(HPC) runs AI-driven data cleaning applications to process and
refine this data. The cleaned output is written back to object storage,
which is again copied to the file storage system. This traditional
workflow introduces several challenges, including data duplication,
synchronization issues, performance bottlenecks, and inefficiencies
in storage management, as well as unnecessary operational costs
arising from the reliance on two separate storage systems.
To mitigate these challenges, the media enterprise used a data
lakehouse architecture, which combines the strengths of both high-
performance, distributed file systems and object storage. This uni-
fied storage platform enables concurrent access to data as both
files and objects, eliminating the need for data replication and syn-
chronization. Additionally, sustainability practices are integrated
into the design to ensure that the data lakehouse is energy-efficient
and optimized for long-term operational sustainability. This can be
achieved using different technologies such as hierarchical storage
management (HSM) technologies combined with the use of infor-
mation lifecycle management policies, placing data on appropriate
media types based upon age, access time and size [6].
This paper aims to detail the approaches [see 1, 1] employed to im-
plement a data lakehouse solution that addresses these challenges.
Furthermore, we will explore the innovative reference storage ar-
chitecture of a leading research organization which employs several
features described in the Reference Architecture for Research Data
[5], along with some sustainability approaches described in this
paper. This solution demonstrates a balance of flexibility, perfor-
mance, and sustainability [6]. Moreover, generative AI training jobs
could greatly benefit from such a solution, as the size of datasets
for AI training continues to grow, the ability to quickly bring data
online or offline to meet different needs will be crucial.
The following sections provide detailed information into the
various approaches for achieving a sustainable, high-performance
storage solution for HPC and AI.
3.1
Sustainable Energy
According to Gartner’s recent survey results [7], sustainability has
consistently remained among the top 10 business priorities. In
addition, leading CEOs are using sustainability to drive business
growth as sustainable products and services have higher demand.
Some key considerations for achieving sustainable energy usage
include:
1. ENERGY STAR Products: Utilize ENERGY STAR certified
processors and storage equipment from vendors such as IBM,
Intel, and others.
2. Storage Device Selection for Cold/Hot Data: Using stor-
age devices based on data usage frequency, such as employ-
ing RAID 5, SSDs, near-line SAS disk, spin-down disk, or
tape storage for hot or cold data storage, as appropriate.

3.2
Efficient Cooling and Heat Reuse
Some key considerations for achieving energy efficiency in systems
include:
1. Dynamic Cooling Systems: Use cooling systems that can
adapt to changes in temperature in the infrastructure setup.
For example, utilize outside air for cooling whenever feasible,
thereby reducing the need for energy-intensive mechanical
cooling [8].
2. Modern Low-Power Hardware: Selection of appropriate
low-power hardware in storage servers to minimize energy
consumption without compromising performance.
3. Liquid Cooling: Liquid cooling can reduce the power re-
quirements of servers and improve their performance due
to more efficient thermal management [9].
4. Heat Reuse: Consider strategies for repurposing waste
heat generated by data center operations. For example, IBM
built a data center in Switzerland which repurposed excess
heat to warm a nearby swimming pool [10], showcasing an
innovative approach to energy reuse.
3.3
Optimized Storage for Reduced Energy
Consumption and Space Utilization
Space Efficiency: Optimizing storage, whether by increasing stor-
age capacity per rack or utilizing more advanced storage systems,
allows for more data to be stored within a smaller number of racks.
This reduction in rack count leads to a smaller overall physical
footprint.
Energy Reduction: More compact or efficient storage racks
reduce the amount of floor space that needs to be cooled or illumi-
nated, resulting in significant energy savings across the facility.
3.4
High-Performance Data Access
High-performance storage solutions are critical for managing the
increasing volume, variety, and velocity of data, especially in high-
demand fields such as Generative AI and High-Performance Com-
puting (HPC). In the AI domain, the use of GPUs for accelerated data
processing highlights the need for high-performance storage as a
fundamental requirement. Storage systems designed for scalability
may provide low-latency access and high-throughput capabilities to
effectively handle massive datasets while maintaining operational
efficiency.
Such systems should support tunable configurations, enabling
administrators to scale processing capacity up or down as needed,
ensuring consistent data access speeds and reliability even as work-
loads fluctuate. High-performance storage with scalability enables
enterprises to manage and analyze vast volumes of unstructured
data without compromising performance, facilitating the execution
of complex algorithms and real-time analytics across both file and
object protocols. In addition, a high-performance storage system
reduces data access time, leading to faster processing and less re-
liance on extended computational resources. This efficiency not
only accelerates workflows but also helps minimize energy con-
sumption by optimizing the use of hardware and reducing the need
for prolonged GPU usage for generative AI jobs. By leveraging
technologies such as global data fabrics and data lakehouses, high-
performance storage systems offer enhanced flexibility, resilience,
and speed—essential for enterprises addressing the challenges of
next-generation AI and data-intensive workloads.
For example, data lakehouse based on IBM watsonx.data can
leverage IBM Storage Scale [11] which offers high-performance data
access. The recent performance test data [12] for object (S3) access
of data with IBM Storage Scale, show that the bandwidth measured
with S3 for reading large objects is 63 GB/s and 24 GB/s for writes.
The tests were conducted using COSBench, and it was observed that
CPU utilization increased with the number of COSBench workers
increasing, starting with minimal utilization for 1 and 8 workers,
and peaking with higher utilization as the number of workers grew.
3.5
Unified File and Object Storage Access
Operating file and object storage as distinct systems requires in-
creased hardware and therefore greater energy consumption. This
increases environmental impact and cost, creating a workflow that
involves complex – often manual – data management and dupli-
cation. Consolidating file and object storage into a single unified
system can address these challenges and offer several key benefits,
including:
1. Reduced Storage Costs and Elimination of Data Silos
2. Unified Access to Data as Both Files and Objects
3. Streamlined Data Management via a Global Namespace
4. Improved Performance
5. Seamless Integration of Legacy Applications into the Object
Storage Environment
3.6
Multi-tenancy Support
Systems that support multiple tenants benefit from aggregation
of overheads. The reduction in waste leads to more sustainable
computing through:
1. Improved Resource Utilization: Sharing the same physical
infrastructure reduces the need for extra servers, reducing
procurement costs and the generation of e-waste.
2. Lower Energy Consumption: By consolidating workloads
on fewer physical machines, multi-tenant environments use
less power for computing and cooling.
3. Reduced Infrastructure: With fewer servers needed, data
centers require a smaller physical footprint, reducing require-
ments for room cooling, building space, racks and auxiliary
infrastructure and thus minimizing environmental impact
and costs [13].
4. Efficient Cooling: Shared infrastructure allows tenants to
share the cost of investment in cooling systems that improve
overall energy consumption, lowering the environmental
impact of temperature control.
5. Cloud Sustainability: Cloud is an inherently multi-tenant
environment. Many cloud providers have sustainability pro-
grams that take advantage of renewable energy and carbon
offset programs, which help reduce the carbon footprint for
tenants.
In summary, multi-tenancy supports green computing by opti-
mizing resource use, lowering energy needs, extending hardware
life, and reducing environmental impact.

3.7
Scheduling and Storage Tiering
3.7.1
Scheduling. Scheduling involves management of computing
tasks, processes, or workloads. Effective scheduling helps ensure
that resources are used efficiently and only when needed, helping to
reduce energy consumption and the need for additional hardware.
Advantages of intelligent scheduling include:
1. Load Balancing: Distributing workloads efficiently across
servers helps to avoid overloading a single machine while
others remain idle.
2. Optimized Resource Usage: Lower-priority workloads can
be scheduled during off-peak hours or when resources are
underutilized. This optimal use of available hardware re-
duces the frequency of running at maximum CPU clock
speed or the lack of availability to run critical workloads,
thus reducing cooling requirements and the need for new
hardware. For example, non-interactive (batch), preempt-
able GPU workloads could be run on idle inference services
during periods of low demand.
3. Energy Saving: Modern systems can dynamically scale com-
puting power based on demand. Intelligent scheduling en-
sures that computing resources (e.g., processors, storage) are
only active when required.
4. Optimizing Use of Solar Power: Where solar energy is avail-
able, batch jobs can be scheduled to run during optimal
energy generation windows [14].
3.7.2
Storage Tiering. Storage tiering organizes data based on its
importance and access frequency, placing it on different types of
storage (e.g., high-performance SSDs for frequently accessed data
and low-power HDDs for less critical data). Thus, storage tiering
supports sustainability in the following ways:
1. Energy Efficiency: Data which is less likely to be in use is
stored on devices with low power modes, lowering overall
energy consumption.
2. Reduced Hardware Needs: SSDs have a higher failure rate
[15] and lower storage density compared to HDDs and Tape,
but substantial improvements in time to first block for ran-
dom access. Tiering data that is not presently in use reduces
the volume of “hot” storage required, and the resultant re-
duction in hardware volume reduces e-waste and energy
consumption.
3. Optimized Resource Utilization: The benefits of low-power
storage are lost when cycles on high-performance systems
are lost due to data recall times. Policy-based data tiering,
along with the ability to recall data prior to computation, fa-
cilitates the use of low-powered storage as a ‘default’ without
substantial delays to high-performance demands.
4. Cost-Effective: Storing less critical data on higher-density,
lower-energy devices reduces the cost per terabyte of data
storage, making data retention requirements more palatable
as datasets grow.
5. Lower Cooling Requirements: A reduction in energy usage
results in a reduction in heat generation, reducing cooling
requirements and the resulting cost and carbon footprint of
data centers.
3.7.3
Combining Scheduling and Storage Tiering for Greater Sus-
tainability. When combined, scheduling and storage tiering create
a powerful system for sustainable computing through:
1. Scheduled Tiered Backups: Data can be backed up or
archived during off-peak hours and stored in energy-efficient
tiers. This reduces energy consumption during peak hours
and lowers operational costs.
2. Dynamic Data Migration: Scheduled tasks can trigger auto-
matic migration of data to lower-energy storage based on
file size, data pool policies, and recency of access.
3.8
Scalability
A scalable storage system is one that can expand in capacity and
performance as data volumes grow, without major disruptions or
performance bottlenecks. To meet the growing [1] demand for data
for AI and HPC, you need to design a storage infrastructure that
can grow dynamically, handle increasing data loads, and provide
consistent performance. Below are the key strategies to consider
when implementing scalable storage:
1. Distributed Storage: Use cloud object storage for easy scala-
bility and cost-effective management of large datasets. Dis-
tributed file systems such as IBM Storage Scale or Ceph
provide scalable storage across multiple nodes and enable
faster data access.
2. Tiered Storage: Ensure that all tiers of storage have the
ability to expand according to requirements and use metrics
to determine which tiers require expansion.
3. Data Deduplication: Apply data deduplication to remove
redundant copies of data and save storage space, especially
with large AI datasets.
4. Hybrid and Multi-Cloud Solutions: Combine on-premises
and cloud storage (hybrid) for flexibility, as this enables rapid
and urgent storage scaling without waiting for procurement
and delivery of new hardware, and utilization of cloud com-
pute resources for computational scaling.
5. Minimal data movement:
Instead of replicating entire
datasets across sites, the data fabric replicates data for a
specific workload. This approach minimizes needs for both
storage and network power, reducing capacity requirements.
A scalable AI and HPC storage strategy can use a combination of
features including cloud-based distributed storage, tiered storage,
high-performance SSDs, and data versioning. This ensures efficient
data management, cost savings, and high performance as AI and
HPC workloads grow.
3.9
Disaster Recovery and Distributed Data
Acceleration
3.9.1
Disaster Recovery. A disaster recovery strategy for HPC and
AI must account for the most critical data and workloads, and for
the high throughput, large datasets, and complexity requirements
typical in these environments. Some strategies to support disaster
recovery for HPC and AI storage are:
1. Data Replication: Support synchronous replication for real-
time replication for critical datasets (e.g., AI models) and

asynchronous replication for regular replication of large,
non-critical datasets.
2. Backup and Snapshots: Take point-in-time backups of im-
portant data and systems. Also take incremental backups to
store only changes since the last backup to optimize storage.
3. Multi-Site and Geo-Redundancy: Store data across multiple
locations (cloud regions or data centers) for high availability.
Use clusters or cloud resources to distribute AI and HPC
workloads for failover. For very large datasets, the time to
backup all data using traditional methods can be untenable
(i.e. the time required for backup is longer than the window
available in which to do it), and archival through multi-site
strategies is required.
4. High Availability (HA) Storage: Protect data from hardware
failure through redundancy. Use distributed file systems
such as IBM Storage Scale and Ceph for fault-tolerant, scal-
able storage.
5. Automated Failover and Recovery: Use automation to mi-
grate workloads to backup resources during failure. Inte-
grate on-prem systems with cloud backup for rapid recovery.
6. Disaster Recovery Testing: Regularly test failover and recov-
ery procedures to ensure quick restoration.
7. Data Integrity: Use hashing to verify the integrity of data
during backup and recovery.
8. Hybrid and Cloud Integration: Combine on-prem and cloud
resources to provide flexible, scalable disaster recovery. Con-
sider multi-provider solutions for critical data.
3.9.2
Distributed Data Acceleration. Data acceleration with data
caching can help to reduce storage access times. This can help to
make AI processing more efficient by reducing the need for repeated
data retrieval.
1. Multi-Site Synchronization: Data acceleration can make it
possible to have seamless data access across sites, by support-
ing features such as automatic replication, real-time sync,
and optimized bandwidth management to avoid bottlenecks.
2. Data Consistency: In multi-site environments, it is important
to ensure that the same data is accessible and consistent to
ease synchronization of data access across locations. This
is particularly important for training AI models on datasets
that must be identical across various instances.
3. Integration with Data Acceleration Tools: Storage systems
should support data acceleration technologies with caching
and compression to enhance throughput and reduce data
retrieval time. This is crucial for AI and machine learning
applications where high-processing speed is required.
Asynchronous File Management (AFM), part of IBM Storage
Scale, enables efficient, non-blocking file access across distributed
storage systems. By managing data seamlessly and asynchronously,
AFM reduces latency, prevents bottlenecks, and allows multiple
tasks to run simultaneously. This reduces storage access times,
especially in multi-site environments that share large datasets, with
benefits including optimized network usage and enhanced data
availability, which are required for AI training applications that
need quick access to large datasets.
4
USE CASE: Global Data Fabric FOR
RESEARCH ORGANIZATION
4.1
Global Data Fabrics Architectures
Global data fabric architectures refer to a cohesive, integrated frame-
work designed to streamline and manage data workload across di-
verse, distributed environments such as hybrid cloud, multi-cloud,
on-premises, and edge systems. An important goal of a global data
fabric is to offer a consistent and scalable automated infrastructure
that simplifies how data is accessed, managed, and shared across
various platforms and geographic locations.
The Research Data Reference Architecture (RDRA) [5][16] speci-
fies some of the key features that can guide the design, construction
and procurement of global data fabrics and data lakehouse for re-
search organizations.
This paper presents a brief use case from a research organiza-
tion that has implemented a storage system aligned with some
approaches discussed in this paper and several RDRA features.
The case study highlights how the organization, while adopting
several features and approaches, has also seamlessly integrated
sustainable storage practices into its infrastructure, reflecting the
growing emphasis on long-term environmental responsibility in
data management.
4.2
Use Case: Data Lakehouse environment at a
Leading Research Organization using
High-performance, Sustainable Storage
Acronyms:
• CES: Cluster Export Services – A service provided by IBM
Storage Scale.
• DMF: Data Management Framework – A comprehensive
solution for managing data storage and migration.
• AFM: Active File Management – A technology that facili-

storage environments.
The Figure 2 illustrates a deployment based on the storage in-
frastructure at The University of Queensland, Australia. Data is
ingested from a variety of sources, including instruments, users, and
from collaborators via cloud services. Depending on the specific ser-
vice requirements, the data is processed either by high-performance
computing (HPC) services or campus services clusters. The data
is transferred to the active storage tier in a data center using IBM
Storage Scale Active File Management (AFM) technology. DMF
replicates data into storage tiers as appropriate for data resiliency
and recall. Additionally, data is moved from the active tier based
on age and frequency of use.
The following key technologies are utilized in this use case:
1. Scalable, High-Performance, Unified Data Storage solution:
The infrastructure utilizes the IBM Storage Scale solution
to provide a highly available, high-performance, and scal-
able storage environment. Additional units of storage can
be easily added to expand storage capacity as needed. IBM
Storage Scale also provides a unified storage solution that
supports multi-protocol data access. This is beneficial as the
storage system accommodates a variety of data access needs;
supercomputers typically require high-performance parallel

This use case demonstrates the application of several approaches
discussed in this paper, including Sustainable Energy, High-
Performance Data Access, Unified File and Object Storage Access,
Scheduling and Storage Tiering, Scalability, and Disaster Recovery.
It also highlights the application of key features such as Scalability
and Versatility, as outlined in the RDRA, underscoring the align-
ment with best practices in research data management.
5
CONCLUSIONS
In this paper, we have discussed various approaches to implement
sustainable, high-performance storage solutions which can be tai-
lored to the specific needs of high-performance computing (HPC)
and artificial intelligence (AI). These approaches help enable next-
generation data architectures, such as global data fabrics and Data
lakehouses, which are increasingly required to address the complex
data management challenges faced by modern research institutions
and enterprises worldwide.
We have highlighted the key factors that influence the selection
of optimal storage solutions, focusing on the need to strike a balance
between performance and sustainability. Factors such as scalability,
high-performance access, energy efficiency, and cost-effectiveness
are essential considerations for building infrastructure capable of
supporting the demanding workloads of HPC and AI applications.
This paper provides guidance for selecting storage systems that
can meet both the high-performance requirements and long-term
sustainability goals of research organizations and enterprises.
Through this analysis, we aim to provide research teams and IT
professionals with the insights needed to make informed, strategic
decisions in planning and deploying storage solutions. The ap-
proaches discussed offer a roadmap for the development of future-
ready storage infrastructure systems that can meet the increasing
performance demands of HPC and AI whilst minimizing the en-
vironmental impact of data centers, aligning with the strategic
objectives of sustainability and efficiency in data management.
